summary: A paper proposing a scheme, called ENCAPS, which the author believes is a good medium-term solution to Internet routing and addressing problems, tied to the IPng effort. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: ENCAPS is a proposed way to route IP packets between autonomous domains. Border routers would add an outer IP header for the source and destination domains, so transit routers could forward the packet without using the inner destination address.

questions: proposals for internet routing and addressing in the 1990s
subtitle: A proposal to route between autonomous domains by adding an outer IP header.

tldr.problem: The proposal addresses Internet routing and addressing concerns and seeks a medium-term approach while longer-term solutions were still being developed.
tldr.mechanism: Border routers add an outer IP header containing source and destination autonomous-domain addresses. Transit routers forward that header, and the exit border router removes it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1955 was submitted to the IETF IPng area as a proposal. Its publication does not imply that the IPng area accepted its ideas.

today: RFC 1955 is an Informational proposal, and the unit metadata lists no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC itself says publication does not imply acceptance by the IETF IPng area.

sections.title: The Medium-Term Routing Proposal
sections.content:
RFC 1955 describes ENCAPS, a proposal first made to the Routing and Addressing group and later submitted to the IETF IPng area. It is presented as a medium-term response to Internet routing and addressing problems while a longer-term solution was still being considered.

The author lists goals including reducing routing table size while avoiding changes to hosts, most routers, and routing protocols. The memo also states limits: the proposal is not intended as a long-term solution in its initial form, assumes current IP addresses remain globally unique, and requires extra processing at border routers.
sections.plainLanguage: ENCAPS is a proposal intended to help with routing and addressing while longer-term options were being considered. The RFC makes clear that publishing the proposal does not mean the IPng area accepted it.

sections.title: Routing with an Outer IP Header
sections.content:
ENCAPS routes between autonomous domains (ADs), groups of networks managed as domains for the proposal. When a border router receives a datagram without an AD header, it looks at the source and destination addresses and uses DNS to obtain the AD addresses. It adds an outer IP header, called the AD-Header, whose source and destination identify the originating and destination ADs.

Border routers exchange routes for these AD addresses. Transit-domain routers forward the encapsulated datagram using the outer header without needing special handling. The final border router removes the AD-Header and forwards the original datagram to its destination. The proposal uses ordinary IP addresses for AD identifiers, with a small number of network numbers reserved for that purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: The entry border router adds an outer IP header naming the source and destination domains. Transit routers forward the packet using that outer header, and the exit border router removes it.

sections.title: Changes and Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The proposal requires DNS to store an AD address for each name. Border routers need to perform DNS lookups, add and remove AD-Headers, and run routing between autonomous domains. The memo says hosts and non-border routers would not need changes.

The stated benefits include separating inter-domain routing from routing inside a domain and avoiding address translation. The costs include additional work at the entry and exit border routers and an extra 20-byte IP header on transit networks. The proposal also says it is not a long-term solution in its initial form and relies on existing IP addresses remaining globally unique for a long time.
sections.plainLanguage: ENCAPS concentrates new work at DNS and border routers, while leaving hosts and other routers unchanged. Each carried datagram gains an extra 20-byte IP header, and the proposal relies on globally unique IP addresses.

sections.title: Status as an IPng Submission
sections.content:
The RFC says it was submitted to the IETF IPng area in response to RFC 1550. It explicitly states that publication does not imply acceptance by the IPng area of any ideas in the document. It invites comments through the mailing list named in the RFC.

The memo describes ENCAPS as a proposal, not as an adopted standard or deployed solution. Its security considerations say that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 1955 records a proposal submitted for discussion. The RFC explicitly says publication does not mean that the IPng area accepted it.

references.text: Gross, P., and P. Almquist, "IESG Deliberations on Routing and Addressing", RFC 1380, ANS, Stanford University, November 1992.
